articles.title: Deploy a Containerized Web App on AWS with ECR, ECS Fargate and an Application Load Balancer (Step by Step)
articles.excerpt: Containers solve the "works on my machine" problem, but you still need somewhere to run them. Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate runs containers without any servers to patch or scale: you describe the containe…
articles.body: Containers solve the "works on my machine" problem, but you still need somewhere to run them. Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate runs containers without any servers to patch or scale: you describe the container, and AWS finds the capacity. In this post I'm taking a small web app from source code to a production-style deployment: the image goes into Amazon ECR , runs as two Fargate tasks behind an Application Load Balancer , and then gets updated to version 2 with a rolling deployment . I measured that rollout from the outside, and not a single request failed.

articles.title: Firebase rules: how to find allow read, write: if true and fix it before launch
articles.excerpt: Firestore and Realtime Database rules decide who can read and write your data. AI app builders often leave the starter rule that allows everything. Here is how to find and fix that. allow read, write:…
articles.body: Firestore and Realtime Database rules decide who can read and write your data. AI app builders often leave the starter rule that allows everything. Here is how to find and fix that. The rule to look for allow read, write: if true; That lets anyone on the internet read and write the collection. Test-mode rules that expire are another trap: when they expire, the app breaks, and people paste in the open rule to make it work. A safer pattern Require sign-in and check ownership: rules_version = '2'; service cloud.firestore { match /databases/{database}/documents { match /users/{userId}/{document=**} { allow read, write: if request.auth != null && request.auth.uid == userId; } } } Each user can only reach their own documents. Add narrower rules for shared data.

articles.title: Is my Supabase database exposed? 4 tests you can run in 10 minutes (RLS checker)
articles.excerpt: Row Level Security (RLS) is what decides who can read your Supabase tables. If it is off, or a policy is too broad, anyone with your public anon key can read the data through the API. Here are four te…
articles.body: Row Level Security (RLS) is what decides who can read your Supabase tables. If it is off, or a policy is too broad, anyone with your public anon key can read the data through the API. Here are four tests you can run on a project you own. Test 1: Is RLS enabled? In the Supabase dashboard, open Table Editor . Tables without RLS show an "RLS disabled" warning. Or run in the SQL editor: select schemaname , tablename , rowsecurity from pg_tables where schemaname = 'public' ; Every table with user data should have rowsecurity = true . Test 2: Do any policies allow everything? select tablename , policyname , cmd , qual from pg_policies where schemaname = 'public' ; A qual of true on a private table means any role the policy covers can read every row.

articles.title: A deployment checklist for small FastAPI and Node.js APIs
articles.excerpt: A deployment marked successful is not the same as an API that is actually serving requests. Our own experimental cloud deployment history included failed and removed deployments; it did not establish…
articles.body: A deployment marked successful is not the same as an API that is actually serving requests. Our own experimental cloud deployment history included failed and removed deployments; it did not establish continuous uptime. Here is the checklist we use to separate deployment status from runtime evidence. 1. Define a simple health contract Choose a health endpoint (for example /health ) with an expected HTTP status and response body. Check it locally before deploying. A health endpoint is a basic liveness signal, not proof that every dependency or business operation works. 2. Separate build and runtime failures Inspect build logs for dependency or compilation errors. Inspect runtime logs separately for startup exceptions, missing configuration and port binding issues.

articles.body: A pair of companies in Europe have signed an agreement to study the feasibility of developing weapons that can be dropped from orbit. Atmos, a space company known for its Phoenix reusable reentry vehicle , will work with MBDA, Europe's largest missile manufacturer, on the new project. "We are assessing how proven defense systems and new orbital technologies can be combined to strengthen Europe's conventional deterrence and enable future defense capabilities," Sebastian Klaus, the CEO of Atmos Space Cargo, said in a statement on Nov. 18. The system that the companies are investigating is called Precision Orbital Deep Strike, or PODS. The companies said that their initial scope will center on design and feasibility, as well as technology integration.

articles.title: Who turned the W upside down? Why Cassiopeia won't sit still
articles.excerpt: The queen in the northern night sky is supposedly one of the easiest constellations to recognize — you just look for a W. Or is that an M?
articles.body: Some constellations are like old friends. You know them well, they're always there, and they never seem to change. A case in point is Cassiopeia, the queen. Its beautiful name comes from Greek mythology — the mother of Andromeda — and its shape is said to represent a queen sitting on a throne. To a stargazer, Cassiopeia is best known as a prominent northern constellation shaped like the letter W. It's easy to find — look north, find five reasonably bright stars making a W, congratulate yourself on finding Cassiopeia and use it to get somewhere more interesting. It's so often a signpost, not a destination. But look north a few hours after dark this month, and you'll notice the W has gone.
